newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says foreign T-bill access not IMF issue.
newsitem.headline: Russia says foreign T-bill access not IMF issue.

text.p: Foreign access to Russia's Treasury bill market is not an issue which could stop the country receiving the next tranche of its $10 billion International Monetary Fund loan, Russian Central Bank Deputy Chairman Andrei Kozlov said on Wednesday.
He said the IMF had objected to the central bank restricting repatriation by non-residents of current earnings from investing in T-bills, as well as restricting repatriation of capital.

"The main and unique problem is taxes. Everything else is a problem to be discussed, but they are not critical. We are now holding technical consultations with the IMF to define what should count as current operations," he said.
Russia has signed up to the IMF's Article Eight on currency convertibility, under which it is not supposed to restrict current flows, although it can restrict capital movements.
"The IMF granted us a respite in resolving this problem two months ago, and we have carte blanche until the end of the year to do everything the way we have so far," Kozlov told Reuters.
"By the new year the central bank and IMF must agree on what will happen next."

An IMF mission left Moscow last month after failing to agree with the Russian authorities on a series of issues, preventing it from making a recommendation on whether Russia should receive the next $330 million tranche of its Extended Fund Facility.

The main area of disagreement was Russia's poor tax revenue performance, but the Fund was also concerned at the implications of the mechanism by which non-residents trade Russian government securities for Moscow's commitment to currency convertibility.
The mission is returning this week for further talks, and Russian officials hope the delayed tranche will be paid.
Kozlov said the issue of non-resident access was not a reason for the delay in paying the tranche.

Since mid-August non-residents have been able to open special rouble "S" accounts at designated Russian banks, and to use funds in these accounts to buy T-bills and government bonds at auctions, and trade in the secondary market.
Non-residents can repatriate funds from these accounts only through forward and option deals with a minimum term of three months.
The Russian banks must offset part of these transactions with the central bank, at special rates which allow the central bank to cap the effective guaranteed dollar yield to foreigners.
The Russian authorities, anxious to avoid a sudden outflow of hot money, say they will gradually liberalise this scheme.
On Tuesday the central bank said it was cutting the proportion of such offsetting deals on spot purchases of roubles to 75 percent from 90 percent.

In mid-October the central bank had already cut the proportion of offsetting deals on forward sales of roubles to 75 percent from 90 percent, at the same time as it cut the guaranteed dollar yield to 16 from 19 percent.
"By cutting the proportion of offsetting deals, we are meeting the central bank's committment to withdraw from regulating this market," Kozlov said.
